newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: INTERVIEW - Fitzwilton upbeat on Safeway deal.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Fitzwilton upbeat on Safeway deal.

text.p: Fitzwilton Plc said on Thursday that a joint venture agreement with Safeway and the transfer of 21 of its Northern Irish Wellworth supermarkets to the privately-owned Musgrave Group would double its net assets and free up cash for strategic investment.

"We will double the net assets on our balance sheet, our gearing will be down to very reasonable levels and we will have the capability of being able to invest substantial money, up to 100 million," chief executive Kevin McGoran told Reuters in a telephone interview.

"By this transaction we effectively got the money back that we paid for Wellworth and in addition we have the opportunity of having 50 percent of this joint venture which has enormous potential over the next few years."

Earlier, Fitzwilton announced that it was setting up a joint venture with the British supermarket group to establish Safeway as a major grocery retailer in Ireland, north and south. The joint venture will acquire and develop 15 of Wellworth's larger stores and four sites in Northern Ireland.
Fitzwilton also announced it was selling the business and business assets of 21 of its Wellworth Stores to Musgrave.
The two transactions will result in Fitzwilton receiving 144 million Irish pounds before investing 10.9 million in the joint venture in which it will hold an effective 50 percent.
It will also receive fees and rents amounting to 8.2 million punts per year from the transactions.
The proceeds will be used to settle certain working capital balances of the businesses to be transferred and to reduce Fitzwilton group borrowings, the company said.

The transactions will also free up cash for strategic investment but McGoran said Fitzwilton would concentrate on its existing businesses - the joint venture with Safeway, crystal and fine china group Waterford Wedgwood in which it has a stake and sign manufacturer Rennicks.
"We are a narrowly-based industrial holding company and in the first instance we will be concentrating on the businesses that we are in," he said.
Fitzwilton said the costs associated with the major refurbishment and development programme to be undertaken by the joint venture would hold back earnings growth in the first year.
"The relaunch costs of the Safeway brand will be 10 million and our reorganisation costs will be nine million.

"Despite that we expect to maintain earnings because we still have revenue from Wellworth, we have rents, we have all our other businesses contributing so we would expect to be able to get through this period of 1997 and maintain earnings," McGoran said.
He said the aim of the joint venture was to establish an all-Ireland retailer.
"We now have 19 stores covering the whole of northern Ireland so that is effectively total coverage of the north. We are now in a position to move south," he said.
The joint venture plans initially to develop into the Republic of Ireland on a greenfield basis, concentrating on the major demographic areas.

"We've already done a lot of groundwork in terms of moving south. We're working on it at the moment, getting sites and developing in key areas," McGoran said, adding the aim was to have at least 20 stores in the Republic of Ireland over the next five years.
